reason: The provided sources contain over 10 cross-validated facts supported by multiple independent websites regarding the dimensions, origins, velocity, and planetary impact of the Local Bubble.
story: Fourteen million years ago, a chain reaction of roughly fifteen massive supernova explosions began blasting away interstellar gas, carving out a 1,000-light-year-wide cavity known as the Local Bubble. As the bubble's shockwaves swept outward, they collected cold gas and dust along the shell, triggering the birth of all nearby young stars within 500 light-years of Earth—including regions like the Taurus molecular cloud. Our Sun was not born here. Five million years ago, our solar system randomly drifted right into the void, leaving traces of supernova-born radioactive iron-60 in Earth's deep-sea crust and ice. Today, the Sun sits almost smack in the middle of this superheated, low-density plasma bubble. Though its growth has slowed, data from ESA's Gaia observatory shows the Local Bubble is still coasting outward at four miles per second, continuing to reshape our galactic neighborhood.
angle: Our solar system is currently drifting through a 1,000-light-year-wide cavity blasted out by ancient supernovas, and every nearby newborn star sits on its expanding outer shell.

claims.claim: The Local Bubble is a massive interstellar cavity measuring approximately 1,000 light-years across.
The Local Bubble was carved out by a series of supernova explosions starting around 14 million years ago.
Approximately 15 supernovae exploded over millions of years to create the Local Bubble cavity.
All active star-forming regions within 500 light-years of Earth sit on the expanding outer shell of the Local Bubble.
The Solar System was not formed inside the Local Bubble, but entered it roughly 5 million years ago.
The Sun is currently located near the center of the Local Bubble.
The Local Bubble continues to expand at a speed of about 4 miles per second.
Supernova explosions that formed the Local Bubble deposited radioactive iron-60 into Earth's deep-sea crust and ocean sediments.
Data from the European Space Agency's Gaia space observatory helped map the Local Bubble's shape, expansion, and surrounding stars.
The gas density inside the Local Bubble is less than one-tenth of the average density of the Milky Way's interstellar medium.
The Local Bubble is filled with low-density plasma heated to temperatures around one million degrees Kelvin.
The Taurus molecular cloud is one of the young star-forming regions situated on the surface of the Local Bubble.
The Solar System currently sits inside a smaller region of gas within the Local Bubble called the Local Interstellar Cloud.

disputed: S5 mentions that up to 1,000 supernovas formed the bubble, whereas S1, S4, S6, and S7 attribute it to around 15 (or 14 to 20) supernovas; the script should stick to the consensus figure of about 15 supernovas.

S1 notes an older hypothesis that a single supernova (Geminga pulsar) created the bubble, but states current research favors multiple supernovae in stellar moving groups; the script should focus on the consensus of multiple supernovae.
